subject: WSJ Economics: Xi Jinping Has Less Leverage Than It Seems

96 Plus, how deficits boost bond yields, AI’s drug-discovery struggles and signs of a food-price shock   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Xi’s Economy Is Failing China’s People   Plus, how deficits boost bond yields, AI’s drug-discovery struggles and signs of a food-price shock   The conventional wisdom is that Chinese leader Xi Jinping meets President Trump today from a position of strength.

   The conventional wisdom is wrong. 

   Yes, China is flooding foreign markets with cutting-edge electric cars at knockdown prices, its robots are beating human sprinters and its AI is nipping at the heels of top American labs. But that technological wizardry isn’t translating into a better life for Chinese citizens.

   Retail sales are a decent barometer of how the typical household is doing and the message is grim: Adjusted for inflation, China’s retail sales fell 0.4% in August from a year earlier. They grew 2.6% in the U.S., and are also up in Japan, Canada, even Western Europe. China’s economy is K-shaped, with capital investment rising in high tech but declining almost everywhere else. Underemployment is pervasive.

         If consumption and investment are flat-to-falling, how can China’s GDP be growing 4.3%, double the U.S.? First, growth is being propped up by exports, because no one at home is buying. Second, China probably overstates its growth. Logan Wright of Rhodium Group estimates China grew 1.5% to 2% a year from 2022 to 2025, not the officially reported 4.6%, and actual growth this year will probably be zero. 

   No elected leader could be indifferent to such malaise. Xi, though, is free to pour resources into advanced manufacturing and tech that lose money and don’t create jobs because, he believes, that will secure China and the Communist Party against outside enemies. The problem: “You become entirely independent of the rest of the world, except for economic growth,” says Wright, author of “Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What It Means for the World.” That gives Trump leverage, if he knows how to use it.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   The bond market cratered Wednesday , with the 10-year Treasury yield soaring to its highest since 2007, after S&P’s September PMI rose to its highest since July 2021 and flashed an inflation warning.

   Another problem for bonds: Deficits raise yields more than they used to, according to Fed economists, because price-sensitive hedge funds account for more buying. These days, a $100 billion increase in Treasury supply raises the five-year yield 3 basis points, the researchers found. (Projected net new bond issuance this fiscal year is $1.3 trillion. You do the math.)

   About 40% of the world’s AI talent now works in China , versus 34% in the U.S., according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. In 2022, the U.S. outweighed China at 46% to 27%.

   Drug discovery is supposed to be where AI delivers some of humanity’s biggest benefits, yet those benefits have been “disappointingly limited,” write Andreas Bender of Khalifa University and 15 co-authors. Few projects by AI-first companies have made it to Phase III trials . In image and speech recognition, AI benefits from plenty of well-structured and well-labeled data. But biological data are conditional, inconsistent and of varying quality, and practical data sets cover only a fraction of small-molecule chemical compounds.

   A food-price shock may be coming . The OECD notes futures markets see much higher food prices than they did three months ago. El Niño and reduced fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are to blame.

   • Advances in air travel are still gradually shrinking the world. In 2028 Qantas will launch an 18-hour flight connecting New York and Sydney .

Greg Ip
 
Xi’s Economy Is Failing China’s People
 
Plus, how deficits boost bond yields, AI’s drug-discovery struggles and signs of a food-price shock
 

The conventional wisdom is that Chinese leader Xi Jinping meets President Trump today from a position of strength.

 

The conventional wisdom is wrong. 

 

Yes, China is flooding foreign markets with cutting-edge electric cars at knockdown prices, its robots are beating human sprinters and its AI is nipping at the heels of top American labs. But that technological wizardry isn’t translating into a better life for Chinese citizens.

 

Retail sales are a decent barometer of how the typical household is doing and the message is grim: Adjusted for inflation, China’s retail sales fell 0.4% in August from a year earlier. They grew 2.6% in the U.S., and are also up in Japan, Canada, even Western Europe. China’s economy is K-shaped, with capital investment rising in high tech but declining almost everywhere else. Underemployment is pervasive.

 
 
 
 

If consumption and investment are flat-to-falling, how can China’s GDP be growing 4.3%, double the U.S.? First, growth is being propped up by exports, because no one at home is buying. Second, China probably overstates its growth. Logan Wright of Rhodium Group estimates China grew 1.5% to 2% a year from 2022 to 2025, not the officially reported 4.6%, and actual growth this year will probably be zero. 

 

No elected leader could be indifferent to such malaise. Xi, though, is free to pour resources into advanced manufacturing and tech that lose money and don’t create jobs because, he believes, that will secure China and the Communist Party against outside enemies. The problem: “You become entirely independent of the rest of the world, except for economic growth,” says Wright, author of “Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What It Means for the World.” That gives Trump leverage, if he knows how to use it.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter, your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What I’m Following

 

The bond market cratered Wednesday, with the 10-year Treasury yield soaring to its highest since 2007, after S&P’s September PMI rose to its highest since July 2021 and flashed an inflation warning.

 

Another problem for bonds: Deficits raise yields more than they used to, according to Fed economists, because price-sensitive hedge funds account for more buying. These days, a $100 billion increase in Treasury supply raises the five-year yield 3 basis points, the researchers found. (Projected net new bond issuance this fiscal year is $1.3 trillion. You do the math.)

 

About 40% of the world’s AI talent now works in China, versus 34% in the U.S., according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. In 2022, the U.S. outweighed China at 46% to 27%.

 

Drug discovery is supposed to be where AI delivers some of humanity’s biggest benefits, yet those benefits have been “disappointingly limited,” write Andreas Bender of Khalifa University and 15 co-authors. Few projects by AI-first companies have made it to Phase III trials. In image and speech recognition, AI benefits from plenty of well-structured and well-labeled data. But biological data are conditional, inconsistent and of varying quality, and practical data sets cover only a fraction of small-molecule chemical compounds.

 

A food-price shock may be coming. The OECD notes futures markets see much higher food prices than they did three months ago. El Niño and reduced fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are to blame.

• Higher global interest rates threaten to drag down housing prices. (The Economist)
